answer.answer:
Site safety is not something the robot delivers on its own: the one cited route into Improve site safety (VA13) in this material is prefabrication/off-site (PR2), that is, moving the work off the site rather than automating it in place, and that route itself requires precise up-front planning and regulatory compliance before it pays back. A second, separate line runs through human-robot interaction (CO6), which reduces contact-injury risk where people and machines share the work, but only if workforce training and robot safety standards are addressed first. Note that only one cited path leads to site safety, so treat the rest of what follows as supporting rather than as alternative routes. The deployed records here confirm safety as an adoption motive but do not, in what is in front of me, carry firm names or enabler codings.

**The one cited route to site safety**

Improve site safety (VA13) carries exactly one inbound and no outbound dependency edges, so the cited causal picture is narrow: VA13 has 1 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, and 39 of the 50 coded cases draw on it [1]. That single inbound edge is DEP19: prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enables Improve site safety (VA13), because moving work offsite improves site safety, on peer-reviewed evidence [2]. Prefabrication is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases [1], so it is a common but not universal move, against a safety value present in 39.

**What prefabrication itself requires**

PR2 is upstream of safety but downstream of several things, and these differ sharply in how widely they are used:

- PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning", because prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1]; RI14 is drawn on by 36 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", since a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [1]; RI18 is drawn on by only 12 cases [1], three times less often than precise planning.
- Three enablers feed into it: PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" enables PR2, orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [1] (15 cases [1]), CO11 "Early contractor involvement" enables PR2, because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in early design [1] (14 cases [1]), and VA14 "Integrate supply chain" enables PR2, supporting the offsite production line [1] (14 cases [1]).

All of these preconditions are organisational or procedural. None of them is a machine, which is the practical point: the safety gain is bought by design and delivery decisions, not by robot choice.

**The separate route through human-robot interaction**

Where work stays on site, the relevant target is a different node. CO6 "Human-robot interaction" mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern", through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits, on standards evidence [1]. That route has two hard preconditions: CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", since the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1], and CO6 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", as collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [1]. CO6 is drawn on by 32 of the 50 coded cases [1] and RI6 by 44 [1], the widest of any enabler discussed here, while RI20 appears in 13 [1]. Training, in other words, is near-universal in the coded record; formal regulatory engagement is not.

**Deployed record**

Three deployed processes in this context name safety as an adoption driver, though none of them is linked here to VA13 or to any other enabler, and no firm is named for any of them: census_RXM1-3, adopted to address safety and market, performs digging and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8 [3]; census_RXM4-5, adopted to address safety and labor, performs digging and material handling on sitework, substructure and foundation, at technology readiness level 8 [4]; and census_RXM23-1, adopted to address safety, performs drilling on the structural core and sitework, at technology readiness level 7 [5]. All three replace people in excavation, handling or drilling, which is the on-site counterpart of the offsite logic: remove the worker from the hazardous operation. They do not evidence the prefabrication route, and the context holds no deployed case coded to PR2 for this question.

**What to watch**

The strong statistical neighbours of Improve site safety are correlations, not mechanisms: VA13 co-occurs with RE6 in 39 cases, with VA2 in 39, with RI8 in 37, with VA16 in 37 and with RI6 in 36 [1]. Read those as company that safety keeps, not as levers. Note also that VA13 applies in the Structural Construction phase, in a value-realizing role [6], so the safety return is booked during structural work even though the decisions that produce it, DfMA, early contractor involvement and supply chain integration, are taken far earlier. Finally, prefabrication is not a single-purpose move: PR2 also enables VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency", VA3 "Improve quality/performance" and VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" [1], which is how it is normally justified. These are the cited edges reaching VA13 and CO6 by exact lookup; the co-occurrence and one-hop material around them is a selection, so it does not establish that no other safety route exists in the wider record.
